repos.title: Catalyzing Interactive HTML Generation Capabilities via High-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning
repos.paper_summary: WebCatalyst is a browser-interaction reinforcement learning framework that trains code LLMs to generate interactive HTML, with mini-games as the main test domain. The policy is optimized with GRPO. Each generated page is run in a browser by an execution agent, and its reward combines three parts. A hierarchical GUI judge aggregates step-level screenshot assessments into a page score from 0 to 100. Visual Anchor penalizes pages whose screenshots are visually worse than a reference screenshot. Action-Trace Credit records JavaScript call stacks for successful actions, maps them to generated tokens, and scales token-level advantages by call depth. The base model is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, trained on fewer than 1K requests, including 640 game requests. On Cookie-Bench Mini Games, the total score rises from 68.8 to 75.3. On WebGen-Bench, accuracy rises from 48.8 to 56.9. WebCatalyst's average rank is 4.0, compared with 4.7 for Claude-Opus-4.7, but GPT-5.5 has a better average rank of 2.1 in the same table. Limitations: only direct generation is optimized, not planning, debugging, or tool use; RL depends on capabilities already present in the base model; and the effects of training data mixture are not studied.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Interactive HTML quality depends on behavior during use, so the paper uses mini-games as a harder test.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work evaluates interactive HTML or trains on webpages, but rarely uses interactive assessors as reinforcement-learning feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: WebCatalyst combines an interactive assessor, a reference-based visual penalty, and call-trace token credit in one policy update.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: WebCatalyst raises WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9 and reaches average rank 4.0 against 4.7 for Claude-Opus-4.7.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Fewer than 1K requests, mostly mini-games, improved mini-game generation and transferred to webpage tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limits include direct generation only, dependence on base-model capabilities, and training on game prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers the GUI Assessor pipeline, trace-to-token mapping, judge selection, prompts, and comparison figures.

repos.title: RAGCompass: Generalizable Retriever Routing via Reranking
repos.paper_summary: RAGCompass is a retriever router for retrieval-augmented generation. Given a query and the passage sets from five retrievers (dense, BM25, SPLADE-v3, ColBERTv2, HippoRAG2), it fine-tunes a Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B to score each passage set. Training uses KL divergence against a target distribution built from the answer F1 each set yields with a fixed Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct reader. A two-layer transformer comparison head, with no retriever-specific parameters, reads all candidate representations jointly. On four QA datasets, test answer F1 is 0.3552, versus 0.2782 for the best fixed retriever and 0.3203 for static-weight mixing. The fine-tuned scorer alone reaches 0.3412, and the head adds 1.4pp. The oracle reaches 0.7508. Recall@5 rises 5.0 points. On held-out corpus, retriever, and reader splits, RAGCompass keeps most of its gain, while three query-only routers do not beat the best fixed retriever. Limitations: one reader plus one alternative reader, retrieval depth fixed at k=5, one reranker size, reimplemented baselines, and a 3.9% decision overhead measured on one device that excludes running all retrievers.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Retriever choice varies by query, and an oracle picking per query reaches 0.75 F1 against 0.28 for the best fixed retriever.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior routers read queries or retriever identities rather than retrieved passages, and none was tested under a shift.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Routing is cast as reranking evidence sets, with a reranker trained to match the answer F1 each set yields.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Five retrievers are routed across four question-answering datasets, with generalization tested by holding out a dataset, a retriever, or the reader.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: RAGCompass reaches 0.3552 test F1, +7.7pp over the best fixed retriever and +3.5pp over the strongest baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Utility supervision beats relevance supervision by 2.11pp, while score coupling changes results by less than seed noise.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: RAGCompass outperforms every compared router at 3.9% of generation pipeline cost and keeps most of its gain under unseen conditions.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results rest on one reader, one retrieval depth, one backbone scale, and reimplemented baselines, so transfer is untested beyond those.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers encoding and head ablations, retrieval metrics, majority vote, depth and data-size checks, baseline details, per-dataset results, and language-model router costs.

repos.title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers
repos.paper_summary: This paper introduces Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD) and Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD) for few-step distillation of multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs). The authors apply both to build NitroFusion2 from Z-Image-Turbo. TSAD attaches discriminator heads to intermediate text-token states, which depend on the image through joint attention. ACD conditions the frozen discriminator backbone on one of six image-grounded fields (typography, object, style, background, action, layout) or on the full caption, sampled per training step. At one step, NitroFusion2 scores 43.34 on LongText-EN and 47.78 on LongText-CN, versus 29.18 and 36.85 for TwinFlow. It scores 86.48 on DPG-Bench, above 84.86 for eight-step Z-Image-Turbo, and 75.86 on GenEval, versus 75.01. At two steps, Z-Image-Turbo++ scores higher on some metrics but uses 12B parameters, versus 6B here. Limitations: one-step output still struggles with complex scenes, sample diversity drops, ACD shows a seesaw effect across aspects, and layer selection is empirical.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Adversarial distillation has read only image features, and MMDiT text tokens offer an unused alternative.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work conditions discriminators on text but reads adversarial features only from the image.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: TSAD attaches heads to text-stream attention outputs, and ACD picks one aspect cue per training step.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: At one step, NitroFusion2 leads all five benchmarks and is on par with an eight-step reference on GenEval.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Remaining limits are complex scenes at one step, reduced sample diversity, and a seesaw effect across cues.

digest_headlines.heading: AI use statement
digest_headlines.headline: The AI use statement says generative tools supported data, implementation, drafting and figures, not hypotheses or framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Reproducibility statement
digest_headlines.headline: The reproducibility statement points to method sections, training setup, cue list, pseudo-code, and public release upon acceptance.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the training setup, cue categories, layer choices, per-dimension results, and open-weight comparisons.

repos.title: NanoKV: High-Ratio KV Cache Compression for Autoregressive Video Generation
repos.paper_summary: NanoKV is a frozen-backbone framework for high-ratio compression of the historical key-value (KV) cache in autoregressive video generation. It stores shared content in cluster centers and encodes joint head-channel residuals into INT4 coefficients. Keys and Values get different fitting objectives: Key decoders are trained with block-output alignment to preserve downstream block outputs, and Value codecs are trained through the quantization path to reconstruct residuals. The optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention. Evaluation covers HY-WorldPlay, Matrix-Game 3.5, and LingBot-World 2.0, using 400 videos per configuration from 100 VBench-I2V images with four camera actions each. On HY-WorldPlay at nominal 32× compression, NanoKV reaches 26.09× effective KV compression, versus 13.50× for KVTC, with PSNR 19.56 dB against 18.56 dB for KVTC. NanoKV-Fast reaches 20.53× with 19.04 dB PSNR and a 1.06× speedup over Original, versus 0.92× for KVTC. Fidelity is measured against matched uncompressed rollouts, not ground truth. The codecs are fitted per backbone, and NanoKV-Fast's low-dimensional approximation may accumulate errors over long horizons.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Growing KV history raises memory and attention costs, so NanoKV compresses historical KV while preserving downstream generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work selects history tokens, compresses features, or changes the model; NanoKV compresses retained features with a frozen backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Joint head–channel compression retains the most KV variance, and Key block-output alignment reduces mean output error by 15.3%.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: NanoKV stores shared centers and low-bit residual coefficients, fitting Key decoders by block-output alignment and Value codecs through quantization.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV reaches 26.09× effective compression and 19.56 PSNR, against 13.50× and 18.56 for KVTC.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: NanoKV improves the quality–storage trade-off across three backbones, but codec fitting and attention adaptation remain backbone-specific.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers cache and baseline protocols, codec training and error diagnostics, memory and runtime accounting, and additional quality and example figures.

repos.title: A 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and segmentation
repos.paper_summary: HoloCT is a 3D foundation model that performs CT interpretation and voxel-level segmentation in one multimodal language model. Two parallel encoders supply whole-volume and fine-grained spatial tokens to the language model, and its segmentation tokens drive a mask decoder that returns 3D masks alongside text. It is trained on HoloDATA: 195,921 CT scans from 73 public datasets and six clinical cohorts, with 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT–mask pairs. Across 346 tasks, HoloCT-8B reaches mean Dice 0.816 on 272 internal segmentation categories, versus 0.799 for 82 dataset-specific nnU-Net models. For multi-target screening, macro F1 rises from 0.368 (nnU-Net) to 0.718 internally. On CT-RATE closed-ended VQA, accuracy is 93.4% versus 84.7% for HuluMed-32B. In multicentre validation on 11,455 scans, thyroid and colon screening reaches 85.1% mean accuracy, above four radiologists in a retrospective reader study. Limitations: finding-level masks cover only chest CT; musculoskeletal bone lesions and diffuse chest findings segment less accurately; volumes are interpreted independently; and hospital validation was retrospective and within one country.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing CT models separate report text from 3D segmentation, so findings are hard to verify spatially.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: A single HoloCT model outperforms specialist and foundation models across 346 tasks, including clinical cohorts.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Mask-paired training and grounded outputs improve interpretation, but evaluation is retrospective and single-country.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: HoloCT couples dual-scale visual encoders with a multimodal language model and mask decoder, trained in three stages.

repos.title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
repos.paper_summary: ServerBench is a benchmark for how well LLM coding agents design complete, specialized LLM serving systems under a shared economic objective: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost, which the authors call "dollars per dollar." Agents start from a minimal Transformers server, have an 8-hour development budget, and their submissions are rebuilt in a fresh deployment and replayed on held-out seeds. Workloads are replays of recorded coding-agent sessions with shared prefixes, multi-turn structure, and parallel subagent branches, and latency targets are the p90 TTFT and TPOT of a frozen SGLang reference. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments (Gemma E4B, Qwen3.5 9B, Qwen3.8 27B INT4), 22 of 33 runs produced verified systems and 13 exceeded the strongest baseline. Claude Sonnet 5.5 scored 2.97 on Gemma E4B, 4.87× the vLLM reference. The authors report three findings: high-value designs raise capacity before adding load, agents interpret feedback better when tests use workload-relevant inputs, and verification must cover the execution paths that optimizations add. Limitations include one coding-trace source, closed-loop rather than open-loop replay, and single runs per agent-deployment pair.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: ServerBench asks coding agents to build complete LLM serving systems and scores them by latency-qualified value per GPU dollar.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks test kernels, patches, or servers under preset conditions, lacking stateful workloads and cost-based objectives.

digest_headlines.heading: ServerBench
digest_headlines.headline: Each task fixes the model, GPU allocation, and workload, and scores verified systems by dollars per dollar of qualified token value.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Claude Sonnet 5.5 reaches 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, and 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Substantial gains come with uneven delivery, pointing to three priorities for agent-built serving systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover three deployments and one trace source, and closed-loop replay with correlational analysis limits generalization and causal claims.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Recorded sessions are reconstructed without original content, generated code runs in isolated environments, and review does not prove safety.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists deployment calibration, replay records, verification settings, integrity review, controlled comparisons, and finding-guided experiments.

repos.title: Spatial-UMI-Dream: Scaling World Action Models with Metric Geometry for UMI Manipulation
repos.paper_summary: Spatial-UMI-Dream is a 5B-parameter World Action Model that jointly predicts future RGB, fisheye-aligned metric depth, and robot actions for Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) data. Depth comes from stereo matching on each gripper's middle and right cameras (Fast FoundationStereo), encoded as color-mapped images and stacked with RGB into a dual-gripper canvas processed by the pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone. Training has two stages: world-only adaptation on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data, then joint world-action training with a weighted flow-matching loss. The authors also introduce RoboTwin-UMI, a 20-task simulation benchmark that varies embodiment (Aloha-AgileX vs. ARX-X5) and lighting. On RoboTwin-UMI, the model reaches 79.10% in-domain success and 72.15% under combined shifts, 4.65 and 10.30 percentage points above the strongest baseline in each setting. Across six real-world bimanual tasks it reaches 85.0% average success, versus 60.8% for π0.5. RGB-only pretraining lowers in-domain simulation success by 5.75 points. Limitations: real-world results use 20 episodes per task, and the simulation comparison uses one training demonstration set of 50 clean Aloha demonstrations per task.

digest_headlines.heading: INTRODUCTION
digest_headlines.headline: Moving close-range cameras leave scene scale implicit, motivating metric depth and a benchmark that tests embodiment and lighting shifts.

digest_headlines.heading: RELATED WORK
digest_headlines.headline: Prior world action models leave geometry implicit, while geometry-aware policies use depth as input or as a distillation target.

digest_headlines.heading: METHOD
digest_headlines.headline: A 5B model jointly predicts RGB-D canvases and actions, trained in two stages on filtered, delay-compensated demonstrations.

digest_headlines.heading: EXPERIMENTS
digest_headlines.headline: Spatial-UMI-Dream reaches 79.10% in-domain and 72.15% under joint shifts, with 85.0% average success on six real-world tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: CONCLUSION
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion restates that metric geometry and two-stage pretraining drive gains in simulation and on six real-world tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the training recipe, RoboTwin-UMI rendering and planning setup, and the task tables with step limits and scored stages.

repos.title: Binding Paraphrased Instructions to Encountered Objects in sLLM Agents under Partial Observability
repos.paper_summary: This paper introduces ALFWorld-Para, a benchmark that paraphrases ALFWorld goal instructions while preserving the task, and BINDIntent, a training-free method that binds paraphrased object expressions to labels the agent has already observed. The benchmark has 226 seen-split instructions, 29 paraphrase types, and 6,554 paraphrased instructions. RL-finetuned sLLM agents and prompted LLMs show 21–52% relative drops in success rate (SR), mostly from object synonyms. A 7B agent identifies synonym referents with nearly 80% accuracy but takes the target object in only 20–56% of synonym cases, versus over 90% under original labels. BINDIntent scores observed labels by cosine distance in ConceptNet Numberbatch embeddings, estimates with a Weibull model whether unseen candidates might match better, and substitutes the label into the instruction once binding is likely. It adds 0.4 ms of CPU time per step and no LLM calls. On synonym paraphrases it improves RL-finetuned sLLMs by 17.5–49.1 percentage points (pp). GiGPO-7B's overall SR rises from 61.8% to 77.4%, above prompted Mistral-Small-3-24B at 63.8%. The method targets object synonyms only. The paper does not test action-axis paraphrases such as Question and Hint, and it does not modify the agent's exploration policy.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Paraphrased instructions lower success of reinforcement-learning-tuned small agents, and a training-free binding method partly recovers it.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior robustness studies focus on system-side perturbations, leaving paraphrased user instructions for RL-finetuned agents largely unexamined.

digest_headlines.heading: ALFWorld-Para
digest_headlines.headline: Paraphrased goals cut success 21–52% relative, and RL-finetuned small models lose their edge over larger prompted models.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Object synonyms drive most failures, and agents often fail to take objects they already observed under synonyms.

digest_headlines.heading: Proposed Method
digest_headlines.headline: BINDIntent binds paraphrased object expressions to observed labels by embedding distance and estimated persistence against unseen candidates.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: BINDIntent raises GiGPO-7B overall success to 77.4, surpassing prompted Mistral-Small-3-24B.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Paraphrase failures stem from referent binding under partial observability, not knowledge loss, so fine-tuning alone may not suffice.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The method targets synonym-driven binding failures, leaving action-axis paraphrases and the exploration policy unaddressed.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers benchmark generation, human equivalence checks, codebases, extra per-type results, and ScienceWorld-Para analyses.

repos.title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
repos.paper_summary: This paper presents OpenPerov, a language-model framework for perovskite solar cell research, and PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark written by perovskite experts from 446 studies. OpenPerov Flash is adapted from Qwen3.6-27B using expert-calibrated evidence records from 4,532 articles, through domain-adaptive pretraining, scientific instruction training and answer-style tuning. OpenPerov Pro retrieves evidence and revises selected passages of a Flash answer. On PSM-Bench, Scientific Mastery (0–100) was 87.6 for Flash, first among 13 closed-book systems, and 89.1 for Pro. Structured-evidence adaptation scored 82.3 against 71.5 for conventional question–answer adaptation. On ten post-cutoff studies, Pro scored 88.2 against 85.5 for experts under the experimental-context rubric. In a self-assembled monolayer experiment, the K analogue selected by the model reached a mean efficiency of 26.69 ± 0.27% versus 25.24 ± 0.30% for the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices with the selected contact reached a 27.05% reverse-scan efficiency versus 25.53% for Me-4PACz, and retained 96.74% of reference efficiency after 1,000 h of dark ageing at 85 °C. Limitations: scores depend on expert-written rubrics, the post-cutoff test covers ten studies, and the device results come from one SAM design with small-area cells.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The authors build a perovskite reasoning benchmark and OpenPerov, a model trained on expert-calibrated evidence records.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Flash scores 87.6 on PSM-Bench, first among 13 closed-book systems, and structured-evidence training beats question-answer training.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: OpenPerov leads every PSM-Bench task family, and its selected self-assembled monolayer contact reached 27.05% efficiency.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Methods adapt a 27B model on 4,035 articles, score 800 questions, and test devices under three ageing protocols.

digest_headlines.heading: Data availability
digest_headlines.headline: PSM-Bench, evaluation records and human assessments are public, but literature-derived training and retrieval corpora are not.

digest_headlines.heading: Code availability
digest_headlines.headline: Code for adaptation, retrieval, revision and evaluation is public, with the Flash adapter and Pro retrieval adapters on Hugging Face.

digest_headlines.heading: Competing interests
digest_headlines.headline: The authors state that they have no competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists supplementary methods on corpus construction, training, benchmark protocol, and supplementary figures S18 to S24.

repos.title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists
repos.paper_summary: OmniQ is an expert-audited environment that converts 60 published computational quantum studies into executable reproduction tasks. Each task asks an agent to rebuild the paper's method and reproduce one target figure. A judge agent checks the output against evaluation criteria that the agent cannot see during execution. Experts found reproducibility issues in 18 studies; one unresolved case was removed, leaving 59 tasks. Across five agentic systems and six third-party harnesses, Claude Code with Opus 5.5 reached about 93% success, while DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in DSH reached 68% at under 7 USD per task. The paper also introduces Residual Agents (RA), a self-improving AI scientist that stores expert-verified workflow repairs as experience. RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash to about 85% at 5.6 USD per task, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at about 85% and 16 USD per task. RA was developed on five tasks and evaluated on 54 unseen tasks. Limitations: source inconsistencies that experts could not resolve remain unreproducible, each memory update needs expert approval, and the dataset was revised after expert review.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Computational quantum science needs autonomous discovery, and paper-to-result reproduction is proposed as its verifiable starting point.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Frontier agents reproduce up to about 93% of tasks, and a self-improving agent lifts a weaker model from 68% to 85%.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Reliable reproduction depends on consistent records, and the authors propose extending the approach to other fields and algorithm discovery.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix reviews classical simulation, quantum algorithms, property characterization, agent harnesses and related AI scientist work.
